newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD invites Labour to coordinate EU policy.
newsitem.headline: German SPD invites Labour to coordinate EU policy.

text.p: Germany's Social Democrats want Britain's Labour party to join them in working out common policies for left-of-centre parties to pursue in the European Union, SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine said on Tuesday.
Lafontaine told SPD deputies in Bonn he had already suggested to Labour that they form joint working groups on European policy similar to those the SPD had with France's Socialist Party.

The main German and French opposition parties are markedly more pro-European than Labour, especially on the question of the EU's planned economic and monetary union (EMU). The newly elected government has pledged to be more cooperative in the EU but stressed it is not strongly integrationist.

Lafontaine, speaking at a meeting also addressed by former European Commission president Jacques Delors, said the SPD had coordinated with the French Socialists a pro-EMU resolution it planned to introduce in the German parliament on Thursday.

"That's why we created the working groups with the (French) Socialist Party," he said. "That's why I have offered to the British Labour Party to create the same work groups to find a common approach in all of Europe."
In the draft resolution the SPD wants parliament to debate, the party said EMU had to start on time in 1999 or the EU would risk a political and economic setback.

It said EMU participants must meet the Maastricht criteria "according to the treaty" and added: "As to the monetary criteria, a lot of EU member states have already reached as broad a convergence as the Maastricht treaty foresees."
The SPD draft also argues for a large number of countries taking part in EMU's first wave.
"The bigger the number of countries taking part in the currency union, the better Germany will be shielded within the single market against speculative devaluations," it said.
The draft also repeated standard SPD demands such as the introduction of a jobs chapter in the revised Maastricht treaty and progress on creation of a political union in the EU.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats held an initial strategy session on Monday evening to prepare for the debate and planned further consultations before the session, party officials said without giving details.
